item.title: Global Testing of Gaussian Means by Combining Marginal and Conditional Evidence
item.description: arXiv:2610.40899v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a test of the global null hypothesis of zero means in correlated multivariate Gaussian data by combining marginal and conditional evidence at each coordinate. The conditional tests are based on the distribution of each coordinate given the remaining coordinates. At each coordinate, the corresponding two-sided $p$-values are combined using the Simes method, followed by a Bonferroni correction across coordinates. Because conditioning can either strengthen or weaken evidence against the null, neither marginal nor conditional testing is uniformly preferable. The proposed procedure adapts to their relative strengths while retaining the simplicity of minimum-type global testing. We establish finite-sample control of the global Type-I error under both known covariance and covariance estimated from an independent sample. The latter setting requires a careful analysis of the dependence between studentized marginal and conditional statistics. We evaluate the power of the proposed test through simulations, compare its performance with existing global tests, and illustrate its practical utility using a TCGA carcinoma dataset.
item.dc:creator: Deepra Ghosh, Edgar Dobriban, Sanat K. Sarkar

item.title: What Paid Triangles Identify about Reserve Uncertainty: Information Boundaries in Loss Reserving
item.description: arXiv:2610.41087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Paid triangles identify some components of reserve uncertainty while others enter through modelling assumptions. We distinguish population identification, recovery by free accident-year-level and two-stage second-moment fits, and precision at practical triangle sizes. In a compound frequency--severity hierarchy, the population law identifies the row dispersion governing non-diversifying reserve variance. With one free level per accident year, its profile likelihood attains its supremum only at homogeneity: the levels absorb realised row heterogeneity on every triangle, in amounts and in counts. Anchoring reopens this channel, but supplies only one observation per accident year. On a $10 \times 10$ triangle the anchored estimate remains uncertain by a factor of several. Within-row allocation dispersion survives conditioning on row totals and hence survives free levels. In the predictive experiments, the treatment of mean-structure estimation error separated the procedures by several times more than the choice among plausible variance laws. A law of the correct form improved coverage only when its dispersion came from a prior instead of the free-level fit. On an outcome-free Schedule~P panel, no amount-only procedure approaches nominal coverage. Strongly one-sided misses reveal a displacement of realised reserves relative to the fitted predictive centres that changing the amount-only variance law cannot repair.
item.dc:creator: Robin Van Oirbeek

item.title: Marginal effects for the stochastic actor-oriented model
item.description: arXiv:2610.41122v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parameter estimates of stochastic actor-oriented models for network evolution are notoriously hard to interpret. Especially a comparison of parameter estimates is problematic, both between different models for the same data set and between the same model for different data sets. Effect size measures based on the calculation of marginal effects are proposed as an alternative to standardize the scale of interpretation but can and should not universally erase the effects of differences in scale and heterogeneity. Simulation experiments show how an omitted effect displaces coefficients and marginal effects differently, and an analysis of empirical friendship network data finds that reciprocity and triadic closure reinforce one another when ties are created but partially substitute for one another when ties are maintained, a contrast the coefficients do not reveal.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Gotthardt, Christian Steglich

item.title: Statistical inference for quantile correlation regression with bivariate outcomes
item.description: arXiv:2610.41126v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is increasing scientifically important to recognize, quantify and visualize the dependence structure between the bivariate outcomes. In this paper, we investigate conditional dependence using a new dependence measure, the quantile correlation coefficient, which is defined by the Pearson correlation of two quantile-hits of bivariate outcomes. Furthermore, we propose a new regression model for covariate effects directly on the quantile correlation coefficient via a generalized linear regression model. The proposed model has intuitive interpretation and provides a comprehensive view of covariate effects across quantiles of bivariate outcomes. The proposed estimator enjoys desirable asymptotic properties including uniform consistency and weak convergence as a process in the quantile index. Additionally, we develop the general hypothesis testing for the regression coefficients, with applications to summarize covariate effects across the quantile ranges. Simulation studies demonstrate the good finite sample performance of the proposed estimation and inference procedures. Two empirical applications of the proposed method reveal interesting insights in premature twins data for measuring association and ChIP-seq data for measuring reproducibility.
item.dc:creator: Feipeng Zhang, Heng Peng

item.title: Balancing Covariates for Continuous Treatments by Exploiting Continuity
item.description: arXiv:2610.41186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider causal effect estimation in observational studies with continuous treatment. We introduce a general class of causal estimands that, as a special case, includes the average causal effect of assigning treatment according to an arbitrary counterfactual distribution. Balancing estimators are particularly attractive tools for covariate adjustment in this setting because they avoid directly modeling the treatment assignment mechanism, thereby reducing the potential for instability and misspecification bias in subsequent causal effect estimation. In this paper, we develop a general framework of covariate balancing for continuous treatment with the proposed class of causal estimands, leveraging the assumption of continuity of treatment dose. As in the binary treatment setting, analysts specify the basis functions to be balanced, the allowable degree of covariate imbalance, and a criterion for selecting among admissible weights. Under a minimum variance criterion for choosing weights, we establish consistency, characterize the effect of basis misspecification, and prove asymptotic normality. We develop consistent variance estimation, which yields asymptotically valid confidence intervals. Under homoskedasticity, our estimator is provably more efficient than inverse probability weighting based on the \emph{true} propensity score. Simulation studies support our theoretical results, and we illustrate the proposed method by estimating the effect of vocational training hours on expected future earnings using data from the U.S. Job Corps study.
item.dc:creator: Souhardya Sengupta, Kosuke Imai

item.title: Source projection for calibrated transfer learning in survival prediction
item.description: arXiv:2610.41230v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transfer learning can improve survival prediction in cohorts with few events. An external model may capture useful covariate associations yet systematically overestimate or underestimate risk in the target population, creating a need for selective borrowing. We propose Source Projection Transfer (SPT) for fixed-horizon prediction with a target generalized additive model. SPT requires only source predictions at target covariates, supporting generalized additive, Cox and neural-network source models without individual-level source data. It projects source log-odds scores onto the target basis and borrows through two separately adapted channels: a projection-centered penalty transfers effect shapes, while intercept-recalibrated soft labels inform probabilities at the target risk level. Under local asymptotics, projection avoids the strictly positive risk cost of estimating an uninformative additional source direction. Each channel asymptotically switches off under its corresponding persistent-mismatch condition. In log-logistic and Weibull simulations with covariate shift, SPT improves mean Brier score and discrimination over target-only modeling in all 24 setting-distribution-horizon combinations. Matched comparisons show improvements over borrowing through source probabilities alone across settings, and over borrowing the complete source score under structural mismatch. In UK Biobank-to-SPRINT mortality prediction among standard-treatment participants with reduced kidney function, SPT improves mean discrimination at 24, 30 and 36 months, with Brier improvements at 24 and 36 months. SPT enables flexible source learners to inform a parsimonious target model while adapting to differences between populations.
item.dc:creator: Fangzhou Cao, Ting Tian

item.title: Instrumental Transfer Learning for Solution Operators
item.description: arXiv:2610.41262v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data-driven learning for the solution operator of a differential equation has broad scientific importance, but observations from a target system are often scarce and costly to collect. Related source systems may provide abundant observations under similar physical conditions, whereas even small changes in the governing equation can induce complex changes in the solution operator, making naive data pooling ineffective. We propose a structured transfer learning method that accounts for unknown sparse differences in the governing equations from a known library of candidate terms. Using the resolvent identity and a whitened instrumental variable approach, we construct unbiased source estimating equations for the target operator. Building on these equations, we develop a three-stage estimator that consists of a target-only ridge pilot, source-wise sparse calibration, and a projected refit designed to remove the leading calibration error inherited from the pilot. An iterative recalibration scheme further reduces the remaining error. We establish non-asymptotic prediction bounds showing when transfer achieves the pooled all-source rate, together with minimax lower bounds that characterize both rate optimality and fundamental identifiability limits under common shifts. Simulations and an electronic band-pass filter application demonstrate clear gains over target-only learning, naive pooling and existing transfer methods.
item.dc:creator: Tongyu Li, Zhuoyuan Li, Ruoxu Tan

item.title: Truthful and Admissible Principal--Agent Testing with Nuisance Parameters
item.description: arXiv:2610.41283v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Statistical contracts reward experimenters according to the evidence produced by a costly study, so the reward rule influences both who participates and what they report. Principal--agent testing theory explains how to prevent ineffective proposals from being profitable. We ask when such contracts can also elicit honest parameter reports if the decision concerns a mean effect but the variance or distributional shape is unknown. Under risk neutrality and a fixed participation cost, we construct menus of e-values --- nonnegative normalized rewards with expected value at most one under every null --- such that (i) agents who know they are null have no incentive to participate, (ii) every alternative type earns positive expected profit and is thus incentivized to participate, (iii) truthful reporting uniquely maximizes expected their reward, (iv) and each contract is admissible: its payouts cannot be pointwise improved while retaining null validity. For Gaussian observations, we treat separately agents who know both mean and variance and agents who know only their mean; in the latter case, truthfulness holds at every variance without requiring a nuisance prior. Multi-sample extensions preserve these incentives and can reward accumulating evidence. Beyond Gaussian models, we show that two independent nonnegative observations suffice to elicit any finite mean above a positive null threshold, without any further distributional knowledge, but one observation cannot combine strict mean elicitation with individual admissibility on this class. Finally, we distinguish the existence of useful tests from the identification needed for truthful contracts. Boundedness is not required, and finitely many null constraints do not by themselves guarantee admissible elicitation.
item.dc:creator: Aaditya Ramdas

item.title: Uncertainty Quantification for Topological Treatment Effects
item.description: arXiv:2610.41593v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a unified framework for uncertainty quantification over filtration scale, extending the topological average treatment effect (TATE) analysis of \citet{kim-lee} to conditional mean confidence and individual effect prediction. For the conditional topological average treatment effect (CTATE), we derive multiplier confidence bands at a fixed covariate value, simultaneous over filtration scale, and prove validity in a correctly specified finite-dimensional regression regime, with explicit control of smoothing bias and nuisance-estimation error. For the individual topological treatment effect (ITTE), we integrate existing weighted and functional split-conformal methods to obtain finite-sample marginal prediction coverage under known target-to-calibration likelihood ratios, with a total-variation bound for estimated ratios. We also extend the current TATE silhouette stability analysis to the diagram-independent bound $\|\Phi_r(D)-\Phi_r(D')\|_\infty \le (1+2r)W_1(D,D')$ for $r\geq1$, recovering the known $r=1$ constant, and propagate diagram approximation error to prediction bands. The installable Python library \texttt{tcda\_uq} integrates mean confidence, individual prediction, and topological preprocessing, with tutorials and reproduction materials. Simulations and a PACCE lesion-measurement application illustrate the distinct coverage targets and the importance of declaring the target population.
item.dc:creator: Hugo G. Souto, Ioannis Diamantis

item.title: Stable and efficient covariance estimation for sample L-moments using H\'ajek projections
item.description: arXiv:2610.41640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: L-moments are useful summary statistics and are widely used in statistical analysis. The joint covariance matrix of sample L-moments not only describes their sampling uncertainty but is also needed for covariance-weighted distances and related statistical procedures. An exact unbiased covariance estimator is already available. However, in our previous applications, this estimator sometimes produced singular or indefinite covariance matrices. Such matrices cause problems when matrix inversion is required. The present paper addresses this difficulty. We examine standard positive-definite corrections and two covariance estimators based on leave-one-out sample L-moments: the delete-one jackknife estimator and an estimator based on the H\'ajek projection. Both are positive semidefinite by construction. Simulation results show that the projection estimator generally has smaller estimation error and better numerical stability than the exact unbiased estimator. The jackknife estimator overestimates the variances of higher-order sample L-moments and has larger estimation error than the projection estimator. We also develop fast rank-prefix algorithms for the three covariance estimators considered. These algorithms substantially reduce computation time.
item.dc:creator: Jihong Park, Palakorn Seenoi, Jeong-Soo Park

item.title: Unidentified prediction-risk rankings under spatial sampling with fixed inclusion probabilities
item.description: arXiv:2610.41726v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For Gaussian spatial prediction, we construct positive sampling mechanisms with identical observation laws and conditional site inclusion probabilities, yet opposite risk rankings for two fixed predictors. The construction selects two of four sites and allows independent Gaussian measurement error.
item.dc:creator: Shinichiro Shirota

item.title: Functional-Specific Information Borrowing under Limited Overlap
item.description: arXiv:2610.41753v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Source observations can improve a target average without estimating the entire shared response accurately. We study this distinction in two independent observational samples whose treatment effects share a rough component and differ by a smoother discrepancy. For power-law treatment overlap known for the analysis, known design density, fixed positive Sobolev radii, and Gaussian noise, we derive matching minimax mean squared error bounds with three regimes. Two explicit source-information thresholds determine the onset of rate improvement and attainment of the source-known rate. A signed local correction explains the thresholds: source observations estimate only the part of the integration functional poorly recovered from the target sample. Direct likelihood lower bounds apply to all estimators. Existing joint reproducing-kernel recovery, which does not require propensity inputs, attains these rates, and standard bias-aware intervals are conditionally honest under the specified class. A supplementary zero-overlap result separates estimation error from residual identification uncertainty. Numerical results illustrate both gains and losses when the total number of participants is fixed. The intermediate rate depends on overlap geometry, while smoothness determines its two endpoints.
item.dc:creator: Shinichiro Shirota

item.title: Observation-Specific Uncertainty Modeling for Latent-Variable Regression in High-Dimensional Analytical Data
item.description: arXiv:2610.41815v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Across many fields, including medical diagnostics, process monitoring, and quality control, decisions often rely on point predictions for single samples. Observation-specific uncertainty is needed to assess the risk of decision error when predictions are compared with thresholds. Latent-variable regression is widely used for such predictions, but observation-specific uncertainty remains difficult to estimate. Traditional methods assume unbiased predictions, attributing prediction uncertainty solely to variance. However, dimensionality reduction can introduce observation-specific bias, violating this assumption. We introduce a framework using Gaussian processes trained on latent scores and prediction errors to estimate observation-specific bias and error variance, separating systematic error from epistemic and aleatoric variance. In Raman measurements of a fructose-sucrose model system, estimated prediction-error distributions agreed with empirical distributions; bias correction reduced mean squared error, and decision limits incorporating bias and variance improved analyte detection over variance-only limits. An aqueous-solubility application using molecular descriptors demonstrated the framework's generalisation beyond spectroscopy.
item.dc:creator: Carl Emil Eskildsen, Georgios Papadopoulos, Kevin A. Giraldo, Mauricio Barahona, Molly M. Stevens

item.title: Unifying Data-Adaptive Longitudinal Treatment-Effect Subgroup Discovery and Pretreatment Membership Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2610.41886v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Precision medicine seeks to match patients with treatments from which they are most likely to benefit. A key step toward this goal is to learn treatment-effect heterogeneity from longitudinal study data. This requires discovering subgroups with distinct treatment-effect trajectories and predicting subgroup membership for new patients from pretreatment information. Existing methods do not fully unify these tasks. Covariate-informed membership models typically prespecify the subgroup number or covariance structure, whereas data-adaptive discovery methods often require prediction in a separate stage. We propose a data-adaptive semiparametric mixture-of-experts framework that unifies longitudinal treatment-effect subgroup discovery and pretreatment membership prediction. Subgroup-specific varying-coefficient functions characterize treatment-effect trajectories, while flexible covariance functions account for within-subject dependence. A covariate-dependent gating model links membership to pretreatment characteristics. A penalty on global component weights removes redundant subgroups, while separate gating coefficients allow patient-specific membership probabilities among retained subgroups. A blockwise generalized expectation--maximization algorithm estimates all model components under a single penalized observed-data objective. We establish consistent subgroup-number selection, convergence rates for the functional estimators, and asymptotic normality for the finite-dimensional parameters. Simulations show reliable subgroup-number selection and more accurate conditional membership prediction than a two-step procedure. Applications to the SANAD epilepsy study and the COMPETE migraine trial identify distinct temporal treatment-effect patterns.
item.dc:creator: Pu Zhang, Yuheng Li, Jiakun Jiang

item.title: Parametric inference for the average hazard approach in time-to-event analysis with sparse risk sets
item.description: arXiv:2610.41935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The average hazard (AH) is a recently proposed model-free summary of an event-time distribution. Over a prespecified window $[0,\tau]$, it equals the cumulative incidence probability at $\tau$ divided by the restricted mean survival time at $\tau$ and can be interpreted as a person-time incidence rate that does not depend on the censoring distribution. The difference and ratio of AHs from two groups, DAH and RAH, are between-group contrasts on absolute and relative scales without requiring proportional hazards. Existing nonparametric inference for AH and its contrasts is based on the Kaplan--Meier estimator of the survival function, and can become unreliable when risk sets become sparse or exhausted near $\tau$, as may occur in stratified analyses. As a practical remedy, we investigate parametric AH inference using Weibull and generalized gamma models. We use maximum-likelihood estimators and corresponding confidence intervals for group-specific AHs, DAH and RAH in both unstratified and stratified analyses. Simulations show that under correct model specification, little bias and near-nominal coverage can be achieved in settings where nonparametric inference is inadequately supported by observed data. We illustrate the method using a randomized trial comparing neratinib plus capecitabine with lapatinib plus capecitabine in metastatic breast cancer. Parametric inference provides a practical complement to nonparametric AH analysis when sparse or exhausted risk sets make inference at clinically relevant truncation times less reliable.
item.dc:creator: Zihan Qian, Lu Tian, Hajime Uno

item.title: A Semiparametric Model Approach to Data Integration under Missing Not at Random
item.description: arXiv:2610.41937v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integrating probability and non-probability samples requires accounting for an unknown selection mechanism that may depend on the outcome. We develop a semiparametric approach in which an unspecified function captures covariate dependence and a scalar tilting parameter governs outcome dependence. Identification follows from an instrumental-variable exclusion restriction and conditional completeness; a zero tilt gives a restricted missing-at-random submodel. We profile out the covariate component and construct cross-fitted, Neyman-orthogonal estimating equations for both the tilting parameter and the finite population mean. The resulting orthogonalized mass-imputation estimator supports centered root-N inference under nuisance product-rate conditions. Its linearization variance accounts for the probability sampling design and estimation of the tilting parameter. Simulations illustrate the cost of flexibility under correct parametric specification, protection against misspecification of the covariate component, and the consequences of invalid instruments or a misspecified tilt. A further simulation using 50,000 national health-screening records finds smaller bias but higher root mean squared error than a parametric competitor under the baseline instrument set. The proposed estimator varies less across alternative instrument sets, although weak instruments and smoothing choices affect precision and interval coverage.
item.dc:creator: Danhyang Lee, Kosuke Morikawa, Jae Kwang Kim

item.title: Co-sufficient weighting: leveraging sparsity for more powerful variable selection in the linear model
item.description: arXiv:2610.42122v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that for the problem of controlled variable selection in the Gaussian linear model, informative and p-value-independent weights (for weighted multiple testing) can be derived entirely from sufficient statistics and a belief in sparsity using only the data itself and no external quantitative side information. Using these weights, which we call \emph{co-sufficient weights} (CSW), in weighted versions of Holm's procedure and the Benjamini--Hochberg (BH) procedure results in substantially higher power than their unweighted analogues when the true coefficient vector is sparse, while retaining Holm's exact validity and BH's highly robust empirical validity regardless of sparsity. We demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed weighted methods compared to their unweighted analogues and other competing methods in a wide range of simulations and an application to HIV drug resistance.
item.dc:creator: Souhardya Sengupta, Lucas Janson

item.title: Identification through Heteroskedasticity in One Lemma: Partial Identification, an Eigenvalue Construction, and a Caution on Rank Tests
item.description: arXiv:2610.41361v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This teaching note unifies known results on identification through heteroskedasticity, under volatility regimes, GARCH, stochastic volatility and covariate-driven variances, in one lemma with a short linear-algebra proof. A shock is identified up to sign and labelling if and only if no other shock shares its variance path, and shocks that share a path are identified up to a rotation. The rows of the structural coefficient matrix solve one generalised eigenvalue problem that nests Rigobon's (2003) two-regime solution. Rank tests on second moments of the errors count at most linearly independent centred variance paths, not identified shocks. A simulation illustrates each point.
item.dc:creator: George Milunovich

item.title: Reliability-Weighted Direct Preference Optimization: Penalized Weights for Robust Preference Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.41588v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) treats every reported comparison as correct, yet preference data contain reversed, tied or otherwise noisy comparisons. RW-DPO gives each comparison an unknown reliability weight $w_i\in[0,1]$ that enters the likelihood linearly -- DPO is $w\equiv1$, a reversed comparison $w_i=0$ -- and estimates the weights jointly with the policy under a minimax-concave penalty on $-\log w_i$. The penalty keeps every comparison the model agrees with at exactly $w_i=1$ and acts only on those it contradicts, through closed-form weight updates at negligible cost over DPO. We prove that recovering all flipped comparisons from a single annotation per comparison requires margins of order $\log n$. Furthermore, in a linear-index model, starting from an initial fit pointing in the correct direction, our estimator jointly consistently recovers the preference direction and weights, as well as identifies the flipped comparisons above this margin scale, even when a fixed fraction of comparisons is flipped. In simulations RW-DPO has the lowest average estimation error among DPO, noise-rate corrections and recent robust methods, with far more precise flags than recent label-correction methods. In DPO fine-tuning of a language model with 10-30% flipped labels, its win rate does not fall as the flip rate grows and exceeds that of DPO trained on clean labels, matching the strongest recent method with corrections concentrated on the flipped labels.
item.dc:creator: Bin Luo, Param Venkat Vivek Kesireddy, Anil Vallepu

item.title: Zero Crossings on the Accuracy-Smoothness Frontier: Maximal Monotone and Minimal Inflection Non Stationary Predictors
item.description: arXiv:2610.41963v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Smooth Sign Accuracy (SSA) framework resolves the smoothness--accuracy dilemma for stationary predictors by balancing mean squared error (MSE) against the frequency of sign changes. We generalize it to non-stationary integrated processes (I-SSA), deriving MSE-optimal predictors constrained by the expected duration between turning points (I(1)) or inflection points (I(2)). The resulting maximal-monotone and minimal-inflection predictors, filters, and smoothers customize classic benchmarks along a new efficient Accuracy--Smoothness (AS) frontier. Tracking the identity (the original data) along this frontier defines the \emph{I-SSA trend}, a novel smoothing concept that, unlike classical filters, imposes no artificial structure on the data-generating process and is directly interpretable through explicit control of turning- or inflection-point frequency. The optimization is a quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP) that reduces to a Generalized Trust Region Subproblem (GTRS) with hidden convexity. On its feasible, invertible region the problem is convex with a well-defined global optimum, and an exact closed-form expression delivers the efficient AS frontier. Under fairly general assumptions, finite-sample solutions converge to an asymptotic I-SSA predictor, devoid of integration boundary perturbations. The framework unifies mean squared error on non-stationary levels, and sign accuracy, zero-crossing frequency, and target correlation on stationary differences.
item.dc:creator: Marc Wildi

item.title: Discovering contemporaneous and lagged causal relations in autocorrelated nonlinear time series datasets
item.description: arXiv:2003.03685v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The paper introduces a novel conditional independence (CI) based method for linear and nonlinear, lagged and contemporaneous causal discovery from observational time series in the causally sufficient case. Existing CI-based methods such as the PC algorithm and also common methods from other frameworks suffer from low recall and partially inflated false positives for strong autocorrelation which is an ubiquitous challenge in time series. The novel method, PCMCI$^+$, extends PCMCI [Runge et al., 2019b] to include discovery of contemporaneous links. PCMCI$^+$ improves the reliability of CI tests by optimizing the choice of conditioning sets and even benefits from autocorrelation. The method is order-independent and consistent in the oracle case. A broad range of numerical experiments demonstrates that PCMCI$^+$ has higher adjacency detection power and especially more contemporaneous orientation recall compared to other methods while better controlling false positives. Optimized conditioning sets also lead to much shorter runtimes than the PC algorithm. PCMCI$^+$ can be of considerable use in many real world application scenarios where often time resolutions are too coarse to resolve time delays and strong autocorrelation is present.
item.dc:creator: Jakob Runge

item.title: The Geometry of Latent Spaces: Projective Invariants, Structural Identification, and Ratio-Scale Measurement
item.description: arXiv:2307.10973v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Latent variable modeling of discrete ordinal data typically relies on Euclidean priors or continuous divergence bounds, inducing a topological mismatch that leaves models vulnerable to factor score indeterminacy, rotational unidentifiability, and Neyman-Scott incidental parameter bias. We introduce an axiomatic, coordinate-free framework that constructs continuous latent coordinate spaces directly from empirical partial orders without extrinsic probability measures. By parameterizing ordinal choice topologies via a regularized log-odds field on a continuous projective product manifold $(\mathbb{P}^1)^Q$, pairwise field differences preserve the invariants of the projective linear group $\mathrm{PGL}(2, \mathbb{R})^Q$. Spectral decomposition of the integrated invariant Gramian matrix reduces the identification fiber strictly to the one-dimensional dilation group $\mathbb{R}_{>0}^Q$. This establishes ratio-scale measurement with generalized specific objectivity, transcending the restrictive uniform-discrimination assumptions of the Rasch model, identically resolving both classical rotational ambiguity and Guttman's factor score indeterminacy. We prove that an indicator array $P \ge 2Q+2$ is topologically necessary and sufficient to anchor a $Q$-dimensional metric space and structurally resolves incidental item parameters without joint, marginal, or conditional estimation. Finally, leveraging Hadamard differentiability and Hanson-Wright operator concentration, we establish that the projective spectral estimator is strongly consistent, asymptotically normal, and achieves optimal parametric concentration at rate $\mathcal{O}_P(P^{-1/2})$.
item.dc:creator: Landon Hurley

item.title: Efficient and Globally Robust Causal Excursion Effect Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2311.16529v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Causal excursion effect (CEE) characterizes the effect of an intervention under policies that deviate from the experimental policy. It is widely used to study the effect of time-varying interventions that have the potential to be frequently adaptive, such as those delivered through smartphones. We study the semiparametric efficient estimation of CEE and we derive a semiparametric efficiency bound for CEE under working assumptions, in the context of micro-randomized trials. We propose a class of two-stage estimators that achieve the efficiency bound and are robust to misspecified nuisance models. In deriving the asymptotic property of the estimators, we establish a collection of easy-to-use theorems for globally robust Z-estimators with either cross-fitted or non-cross-fitted nuisance parameters that are applicable beyond the proposed estimators for CEE. We demonstrate efficiency gain of the proposed estimator compared to existing ones through simulations and a real data application using the Drink Less micro-randomized trial.
item.dc:creator: Zhaoxi Cheng, Lauren Bell, Tianchen Qian

item.title: Partial identification via conditional linear programs: estimation and policy learning
item.description: arXiv:2506.12215v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many quantities of interest are only partially identified from observable data: the data can limit them to a set of plausible values, but not uniquely determine them. This paper develops a framework for covariate-assisted estimation, inference, and decision making in partial identification problems where the parameter of interest satisfies linear constraints conditional on covariates. Bounds on the parameter can be written as expectations of solutions to conditional linear programs with covariate-dependent objectives and constraints that must be estimated from data. Examples include estimands involving joint distributions of potential outcomes, policy learning with inequality-aware value functions, and instrumental variable settings. We propose two de-biased estimators. The first solves the conditional linear programs with plugin estimates and de-biases using standard output from linear program solvers, avoiding computationally demanding vertex enumeration. The second uses entropic regularization to create a smooth approximation, trading a small amount of approximation error for smoothness and computational efficiency. We establish asymptotic normality for both estimators, show robustness to first-order errors in estimating nuisance functions, construct Wald-type confidence bounds, and extend to policy learning problems where the value of a decision policy is only partially identified. We apply our methods to study the effects of Medicaid enrollment.
item.dc:creator: Eli Ben-Michael

item.title: Does Rerandomization Help Beyond Covariate Adjustment? A Review and Guide for Theory and Practice
item.description: arXiv:2512.05290v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rerandomization is a modern experimental design technique that repeatedly randomizes treatment assignments until covariates are deemed balanced between treatment groups. This enhances the precision and coherence of causal effect estimators, mitigates false discoveries from p-hacking, and increases statistical power. Recent work suggests that balancing covariates via rerandomization does not alter the asymptotic precision of covariate-adjusted estimators, thereby making it unclear whether rerandomization is worthwhile if adjusted estimators are used. However, these results have two key caveats. First, these results are asymptotic, leaving finite sample performance unknown. Second, these results focus on precision, while other potential benefits, such as increased coherence among flexible estimators, remain understudied. Hence, in this paper we provide three main contributions: (i) a comprehensive review of the rerandomization literature, covering historical foundations, theoretical developments, and recent methodological advancements, (ii) an extensive simulation study examining finite-sample performance, and (iii) a practical guide for practitioners. Our study compares precision, coherence, power, and coverage of various estimators under rerandomization versus complete randomization. We find rerandomization to be a complementary design strategy that enhances the precision, robustness, and reliability of causal effect estimators, especially for smaller sample sizes.
item.dc:creator: Ant\^onio Carlos Herling Ribeiro Junior, Zach Branson

item.title: Advances in Ontology-Based Mining of Adverse Drug Reactions
item.description: arXiv:2512.11452v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Post-marketing pharmacovigilance is essential for identifying adverse drug reactions (ADRs) that elude detection during pre-marketing clinical trials. This study explores a novel approach that integrates an adverse event (AE) ontology into a zero-inflated negative binomial model to improve ADR detection. By accounting for the biological similarities among correlated AEs and addressing the excess of zero counts, this method more effectively disentangles AE associations. Statistical significance is evaluated using a permutation-based maximum statistic that preserves AE correlations within individual reports. Simulations and an application to real data from the Veneto drug safety database demonstrate that the ontology-based model consistently outperforms classical models such as the Gamma-Poisson Shrinker (GPS). For post-selection inference, we furthermore explore a data thinning technique for convolution-closed families, enabling the creation of independent training and validation datasets while retaining all drug-AE pairs. This approach is compared with conventional random train/test splitting, which may leave some drugs or AEs absent from one subset, and stratified splitting, which requires expanding aggregated counts into individual instances. The data-thinning technique and stratified splitting yield very similar results, with stratified splitting showing a slight benefit, and both clearly outperform random splitting in ensuring reliable and consistent model evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Kenenisa Tadesse Dame, Pietro Belloni, Ugo Moretti, Fabio Scapini, Marco Tuccori, Alessandra R. Brazzale

item.title: Scaling Causal Mediation for Complex Systems: A Framework for Root Cause Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2512.14764v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern operational systems ranging from logistics and cloud infrastructure to industrial IoT, are governed by complex, interdependent processes. Understanding how interventions propagate through such systems requires causal inference methods that go beyond direct effects to quantify mediated pathways. Traditional mediation analysis, while effective in simple settings, fails to scale to the high-dimensional directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) encountered in practice, particularly when multiple treatments and mediators interact. In this paper, we propose a scalable mediation analysis framework tailored for large causal DAGs involving multiple treatments and mediators. Our approach systematically decomposes total effects into interpretable direct and indirect components. We demonstrate its practical utility through applied case studies in fulfillment center logistics, where complex dependencies and non-controllable factors often obscure root causes.
item.dc:creator: Alessandro Casadei, Sreyoshi Bhaduri, Rohit Malshe, Pavan Mullapudi, Raj Ratan, Ankush Pole, Arkajit Rakshit

item.title: Small area estimation using incomplete auxiliary information
item.description: arXiv:2602.12845v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Auxiliary information is increasingly available from administrative and other data sources, but it is often incomplete and of non-probability origin. We propose a two-step small area estimation approach in which the first step relies on design-based model calibration and exploits a large non-probability sample providing a noisy proxy of the study variable for only part of the population. A unit-level measurement-error working model is fitted on the linked overlap between the probability survey and the non-probability sample, and its predictions are incorporated through domain-specific model-calibration constraints to obtain approximately design-unbiased domain totals. These totals and their variance estimates are then used in a Fay-Herriot area-level model with exactly known covariates to produce empirical best linear unbiased predictors. The approach is demonstrated in three enterprise survey settings from official statistics by integrating probability sample data with (i) administrative records, (ii) a cut-off sample, and (iii) web-scraped online information. Empirical comparisons show consistent improvements in domain-level precision over direct estimation and over a Fay-Herriot benchmark that directly incorporates the proxy information as an error-prone covariate. These gains are achieved without modeling the mechanism that generates the non-probability sample: the realized sample is used as fixed auxiliary information, while the working prediction function is estimated from the probability sample under the sampling design.
item.dc:creator: Donatas \v{S}levinskas, Ieva Burakauskait\.e, Andrius \v{C}iginas

item.title: Beyond Vintage Rotation: Bias-Free Sparse Representation Learning with Oracle Inference
item.description: arXiv:2602.22590v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Learning low-dimensional latent representations is a central topic in statistics and machine learning, and rotation methods have long been used to obtain sparse and interpretable representations. Despite nearly a century of widespread use across many fields, rigorous guarantees for valid inference for the learned representation remain lacking. In this paper, we identify a surprisingly prevalent phenomenon that suggests a reason for this gap: for a broad class of vintage rotations, the resulting estimators exhibit a non-estimable bias. Because this bias is independent of the data, it fundamentally precludes the development of valid inferential procedures, including the construction of confidence intervals and hypothesis testing. To address this challenge, we propose a novel bias-free rotation method within a general representation learning framework based on latent variables. We establish an oracle inference property for the learned sparse representations: the estimators achieve the same asymptotic variance as in the ideal setting where the latent variables are observed. To bridge the gap between theory and computation, we develop an efficient computational framework and prove that its output estimators retain the same oracle property. Our results provide a rigorous inference procedure for the rotated estimators, yielding statistically valid and interpretable representation learning.
item.dc:creator: Chengyu Cui, Yunxiao Chen, Jing Ouyang, Gongjun Xu

item.title: Structural identifiability of partially-observed stochastic processes: from single-particle trajectories to total particle density data
item.description: arXiv:2605.13504v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The increasing availability of experimental data has intensified interest in calibrating stochastic models, raising fundamental questions about parameter identifiability. Structural identifiability determines whether parameters can be uniquely recovered from idealised data, a prerequisite to allow for parameter estimation in real-world scenarios. However, there is a lack of methodologies generally applicable to analyse the structural identifiability of such stochastic processes. Therefore, we develop a methodology for a class of spatio-temporal stochastic processes. We investigate how structural identifiability depends on the type of available data, distinguishing between single-particle trajectories and total particle density measurements. For trajectory data, we use a particle-based description that explicitly represents single-particle dynamics. For population-level data, we derive a partial differential equation representation, that describes the evolution of total particle density, and apply a differential algebra approach, common to ordinary differential equation analysis. We further introduce Taylor-series-expansion and Fourier-transform approaches to study the initial condition. We apply our methodology to an example model with a specified class of initial conditions. We show that the model is globally structurally identifiable given infinitely many, infinitely long single-particle trajectories, but only locally structurally identifiable from total particle density data, demonstrating that parameter identifiability depends on the type of data available.
item.dc:creator: Arianna Ceccarelli, Alexander P. Browning, Ruth E. Baker

item.title: Evaluating causal indirect effects when mediators are left-censored by assay limit of quantification
item.description: arXiv:2605.20615v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Causal mediation analysis is essential for disentangling the mechanisms by which investigational therapeutic and preventive agents impact clinical outcomes. However, the measurement of biological mediators is often subject to left-censoring by technical measurement limitations, most commonly an assay's limit of quantification. This form of censoring can pose severe challenges for both identification and estimation of causal mediation estimands, particularly when the censoring mechanism is deterministic and the resulting missingness is missing not at random (MNAR) or nonignorable. Motivated by the question of assessing the role of viral RNA in the action mechanism of monoclonal antibody therapies for COVID-19 in the Accelerating COVID-19 Therapeutics and Vaccine (ACTIV)-2 platform trial, we develop a semi-parametric framework for estimation of the natural direct and indirect effects when the mediator of interest is partially subject to this form of left-censoring. Our proposed strategy combines fractional imputation with a semi-parametric EM algorithm to flexibly estimate key components of the factorized data likelihood. Applying the proposed strategy to circumvent the left-censoring, we discuss both traditional plug-in and asymptotically efficient estimators of the direct and indirect effect estimands, introducing a data-adaptive $m$-out-of-$n$ bootstrap for robust inference under the imputation procedure. We demonstrate in numerical experiments that our approach significantly reduces bias and allows for reliable inference. An application to data from the ACTIV-2 platform trial confirms that monoclonal antibody therapies reduce the risk of hospitalization and death due to COVID-19, while suggesting that changes in viral RNA mediate only a modest proportion of the overall treatment effect.
item.dc:creator: Cong Jiang, Michael D. Hughes, Nima S. Hejazi

item.title: Gaussian-efficient testing by betting on the mean of bounded data
item.description: arXiv:2608.21694v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Given $[0,1]$-valued random variables $X_1,\dots,X_n$ such that $\mathbb{E}[X_i | X_1,\dots,X_{i-1}]= \mu$ for all $i$, we propose a new nonasymptotic confidence interval for $\mu$ that is obtained by inverting terminal e-values generated by a novel betting strategy. When the data are iid, its limiting width matches that of the central limit theorem (``Gaussian-efficient''), finally surpassing the inefficient limits of previous betting intervals. Our main conceptual advance involves designing betting fractions that track the conditional rejection probability of the most powerful terminal test in a limiting Gaussian experiment. When one predictable variance estimator is shared across candidate means, the deterministic inversion is an interval for every data sequence and its two endpoints can be found easily. The width can be improved further with external randomization. In simulations, our method yields the tightest intervals to date; for every distribution tested and all sufficiently large $n$, our deterministic version beats STaR-Bets and is competitive with Gaffke, while the randomized improvement beats both. It thus combines finite-sample validity under martingale dependence, easy endpoint computation, Gaussian-efficient inference for iid data, and excellent empirical performance. We further combine GE-betting with a mixture of constant-fraction bets to attain both Gaussian and large-deviation efficiency under iid sampling while retaining martingale validity. We also extend the construction and its efficiency theory to sampling without replacement, where it again achieves state-of-the-art empirical performance.
item.dc:creator: Diego Martinez-Taboada, Aaditya Ramdas

item.title: Finite-Sample FDR Control for Greedy Aggregation over Networks
item.description: arXiv:2609.14170v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Distributed multiple testing asks $N$ sites, each holding p-values for its own hypotheses, to control the false discovery rate (FDR) of the discoveries made across the whole network while communicating only a small number of bits. Greedy interval aggregation (Pournaderi and Xiang, IEEE TSIPN, 2023) meets the communication budget but controls FDR only asymptotically, and its FDR can exceed the target at finite sample sizes; the same interval counts both select the rejection regions and calibrate the stopping rule, which biases the selected interval densities upward. We propose \emph{budgeted BONuS-GA}: each site mixes synthetic uniform p-values into its data, the center ranks candidate p-value intervals across sites using the pooled counts, and each site's false discoveries are estimated from its own synthetic counts under a per-site share of the level. The procedure needs no knowledge of the null proportions, uses every p-value for both selection and inference, and controls $FDR\le\alpha$ at every sample size for any fixed assignment of hypotheses to sites, assuming only that the null p-values are independent uniforms, independent of the non-null p-values. It keeps the original $O(\sqrt m\log m)$ communication, $m$ being the total number of p-values, when $N=O(\sqrt m)$. We also give a sample-splitting alternative, cross-fit greedy aggregation, with finite-sample control under a random-site model, and we quantify the selection bias behind the original procedure's failure. In a monitoring-network simulation the budgeted procedure retains most of the power of its heuristic counterpart at moderate-to-large site sizes.
item.dc:creator: Mehrdad Pournaderi

item.title: Beyond Pretrends: A Discordance-Based Sensitivity Analysis for Difference-in-Differences
item.description: arXiv:2609.19081v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In the canonical Difference-in-Differences design, the control group's post-treatment change serves as an imputation of the treated group's counterfactual change in the same period, an imputation justified by parallel trends. However, differences in group composition can produce between-group differences in how outcomes would evolve over time, rendering this imputation vulnerable to confounding. An alternative imputation -- such as one based on the treated group's pre-treatment change -- avoids such between-group confounding but introduces the risk of confounding from within-group temporal shifts. Ideally, both imputations, each vulnerable to different sources of confounding, would have concordant values, thereby yielding the same causal conclusions. When the imputations are discordant, conclusions under parallel trends hinge more critically on that assumption since alternative imputations would point to different results. Yet in these scenarios, existing pretrends-based sensitivity analyses can show low sensitivity because they ignore post-treatment deviations from pretrends in the control group. This paper therefore proposes a discordance-based sensitivity model in which parallel pretrends are necessary but not sufficient for low sensitivity. I formally justify this model in terms of the expected distance between the ATT under parallel trends and under alternative assumptions, weighted by the joint plausibility of those assumptions. I then provide a decision-theoretic rationale for benchmarking violations of parallel trends using the worst-case discordance between the parallel trends imputation and alternative imputations. Finally, I apply both pretrends- and discordance-based sensitivity models to assess how a labor supply shock influenced electoral support for apartheid-era policies in South Africa, showing how the two approaches yield different results.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Leavitt

item.title: Fuzzy entropic triple k-means
item.description: arXiv:2609.21538v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper proposes fuzzy entropic triple k-means (FE3KM), an entropy-regularized fuzzy partitioning method for three-way data arrays that simultaneously clusters objects, variables, and occasions. The method combines three row-stochastic fuzzy membership matrices and a full array of block centroids through a product-weighted squared-distance criterion with mode-specific entropy regularization to represent uncertainty in cluster assignments. With normalized product membership weights and weighted-mean block centroids, the ordinary total sum of squares decomposes exactly into within- and between-block components, further attributable to each mode and to individual clusters within each. This identity supports cluster-level descriptive summaries and conditional assessments of the gain associated with each way's partition. We derive a block-coordinate descent algorithm with weighted-mean centroid updates and entropy-based membership updates, and clarify the relationship with tandem procedures, independent partitioning, hard three-way partitioning, and Tucker reconstruction. An accelerated variant is also proposed for large arrays. A simulation study examines partition and centroid recovery under different noise levels and array sizes, sensitivity to the entropy regularization parameters, and a comparison with tandem and independent procedures. An application to a benchmark three-way TV ratings dataset shows how FE3KM illustrates interpretable object-variable-occasion structures and quantifies the contribution of each cluster and mode to overall data variability.
item.dc:creator: Mariaelena Bottazzi Schenone, Roberto Rocci, Maurizio Vichi

item.title: A uniform improvement to conformal risk control via a generalization of e-closure
item.description: arXiv:2610.35821v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We extend the recently introduced e-closure principle for multiple testing to general state and action spaces and to arbitrary, including continuously indexed, families of risks. A collection of e-values indexed by states and risks certifies a menu of actions, and every data-dependent selection from this menu controls each expected loss at its prescribed level. Conversely, every valid procedure is certified by its own normalized losses, which often leave part of the risk budget unused. We introduce a method called recertification, which spends this unused budget. Using known distributional structure, it enlarges the certifying e-values while preserving validity and selects a less conservative action from the enlarged menu. One particularly compelling application is to the popular framework of conformal risk control (CRC) with a known loss family. Here, recertification redistributes unused risk budget among the held-out points of each hypothetical augmented sample. The resulting controller is valid under every finite exchangeable law and less (usually strictly) conservative than CRC. For convex losses on an interval of actions, repeated recertification converges geometrically to an admissible controller. As a second example involving false discovery rate control with e-values, recertifying randomized e-BH yields a closed-form procedure that rejects a superset of randomized e-BH for every realization of the randomization and maximizes the expected number of rejections under the same constraints. Recertifying with the larger e-collection of closed e-BH gives a second closed-form procedure that rejects a superset of the first. Experiments on CIFAR-100 hierarchical classification and simulations demonstrate improved budget utilization and gains in informativeness and power over the corresponding baselines.
item.dc:creator: Tian Bai, Aaditya Ramdas

item.title: Fixed-Horizon Error Rates for Array-RQMC Metropolis-Hastings
item.description: arXiv:2610.36431v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies randomised quasi-Monte Carlo (RQMC) methods for Metropolis--Hastings (MH) algorithms, whose accept--reject discontinuity complicates RQMC analysis. To circumvent some of these complications, we study Array-RQMC for MH, with $N$ replicated chains evolved over a fixed time horizon $T$, where we make use of Hilbert sorting for joint multidimensional updates at each step. For one-dimensional MH and bounded-variation test functions, we prove a sampling mean squared error bound of $\mathcal O_T(N^{-4/3})$ relative to the finite-horizon expectation. For product targets, coordinatewise Array-RQMC Metropolis-within-Gibbs retains this exponent for additive marginal bounded-variation tests, with constants that may depend on dimension. With Gaussian random-walk proposals, the bounds extend to scalar and additive marginal polynomials with an additional factor $(\log N)^\ell$, where $\ell$ is the maximum polynomial degree. For joint updates in state dimension $p$ using $p$ proposal uniforms, we provide a conditional $\mathcal O_T(N^{-1-1/(p+2)})$ framework under regularity assumptions that are not verified for the joint multidimensional examples. Numerical experiments support the verified one-dimensional theory and demonstrate variance reduction for joint Hilbert-sorted updates, including Bayesian logistic regression, while illustrating the limitations of these gains as dimension increases.
item.dc:creator: Jiarui Du, Josef Dick, Zexin Pan, Houying Zhu

item.title: Bias-Aware Guardrail Selection Under Network Interference
item.description: arXiv:2610.36702v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Web platforms use randomized experiment logs to choose budget-feasible treatment allocations while limiting losses to a designated group of units. Under network interference, each allocation requires expected outcomes at treatment-exposure pairs that may be sparsely observed. Existing safe policy selection methods require valid inference for each candidate, but pooling nearby exposures to improve estimability can introduce allocation-specific bias that variance-only bounds omit. We propose exposure-stratified guardrail selection (ESGuard), which aggregates unit-level bias bounds into a bias bound on each candidate's guardrail effect. It incorporates these bounds into simultaneous lower confidence bounds to select an allocation or retain the status quo. Under randomized rounds, a correct exposure mapping, and valid curvature and slope bounds, the conditional bias bound holds in finite samples. With independent rounds and additional regularity conditions, the unconditional probability of selecting an unsafe allocation is asymptotically at most the target level. We evaluate ESGuard on a simulator built from New York City ride-hailing trips. With six months of simulated rounds, we compare estimators that pool nearby exposures on the same logs and candidate sets. Adding the bias bound raises simultaneous coverage from below the nominal 95 percent level to at least 95 percent for every estimator in this comparison. In the underserved-only scenario, ESGuard violates the guardrail in 0.06 percent of its selections, compared with 16 percent for the point-estimate rule under the same gain ranking, and abstains in about a quarter of replications. Omitted spillovers can invalidate the protection. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/esguard-4D2E/.
item.dc:creator: Minkyoung Kim, Hyunjung Byun, Beakcheol Jang

item.title: Conformal ordering: Distribution-free predictive inference for orders and ranks
item.description: arXiv:2610.40340v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study distribution-free predictive inference for the ordering and ranking of multiple unobserved outcomes. Although numerous methods, such as conformal prediction, have been developed for prediction and predictive inference of unobserved outcomes, extending them to provide inference for the ordering of multiple outcomes with an interpretable guarantee is not straightforward. To this end, we develop a framework and methodology for uncertainty quantification in predictive ordering. Our approach begins by reformulating the problem of determining an ordering among multiple objects as a graph inference problem. Our method adopts a multiple-testing-inspired approach and constructs an uncertainty graph, where each edge represents a confidently inferred pairwise ordering. We develop a distribution-free procedure for constructing a consistent uncertainty graph while controlling either the family-wise error rate or the false discovery rate. Moreover, we show that the resulting graphs naturally yield risk-controlling prediction intervals for the ranks of the outcomes. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed procedure achieves the target guarantees tightly while maintaining reasonable power and prediction-interval widths.
item.dc:creator: Yonghoon Lee, Zhimei Ren

item.title: Imputation of Public Opinion Data with Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2606.09351v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely evaluated as simulators of survey responses, yet applied survey research mostly faces item nonresponse. Imputation fills in those missing values to restore the overall structure of a partially observed dataset and has its own well-defined evaluation criteria, which differ fundamentally from prediction accuracy. We present the first evaluation of LLM imputation against proper multiple-imputation metrics and statistical baselines on more than 5 million imputed responses from four public opinion surveys under various missingness mechanisms. We evaluate in-context learning (ICL) for this task by investigating 84 ICL configurations and comparing the best-performing configurations on six open-weight LLMs. The strongest ICL approach improves on zero-shot persona prompting but remains, at best, competitive with statistical baselines (MICE PMM, TabPFN). ICL approaches are sensitive to survey topics and consume 2-3 orders of magnitude more compute. Moreover, prediction metrics commonly used in LLM survey simulation (macro-F1, TVD) do not reliably track imputation quality. Our findings highlight the importance of fit-for-purpose evaluation for LLM imputation, where established multiple imputation remains the better default.
item.dc:creator: Tobias Holtdirk, Georg Ahnert, Joseph W Sakshaug, Anna-Carolina Haensch
